contrast: In American English *a deductible* is also a noun: the amount you pay yourself before your insurance pays (*a $500 deductible*).

senses.gloss: Able to be subtracted from the income you pay tax on.
examples: Donations to the food bank are tax-*deductible*.
Keep receipts for all *deductible* business expenses.
Is the cost of my home office *deductible*?

senses.gloss: Reaching a conclusion by reasoning from general facts to a particular case.
examples: Sherlock Holmes is famous for his *deductive* reasoning.
The course teaches basic *deductive* logic.
Math proofs follow a *deductive* method.

position: both — also after a measurement: *six feet deep*
contrast: *deep* is also an adverb of place (*dig deep*, *deep in the woods*), but for feelings and degree use *deeply*: *deeply sorry*, *deeply moved*, not *deep sorry*.

senses.gloss: Going a long way down or in from the top, surface or edge.
examples: The lake is *deeper* than it looks.
The kitchen drawers are nice and *deep*.
Take a *deep* breath and count to ten.

senses.gloss: Serious and thoughtful, or showing real understanding.
examples: We had a long, *deep* conversation about our future.
She has a *deep* understanding of the law.
That movie was too *deep* for me.

senses.gloss: Felt very strongly.
examples: He has a *deep* respect for his teachers.
The news caused *deep* sadness in the town.

senses.gloss: Of sleep: hard to wake up from.
examples: The baby finally fell into a *deep* sleep.
I was in such a *deep* sleep that I didn't hear the alarm.

senses.gloss: Of a voice or sound: low.
examples: He has a *deep*, calm voice.
We heard the *deep* sound of a ship's horn.

senses.gloss: Of a color: dark and strong.
examples: She wore a *deep* red dress.
The sky turned a *deep* blue after sunset.

senses.gloss: Of trouble, debt or a crisis: very serious.
examples: You're in *deep* trouble, young man.
The company fell into *deep* debt.

senses.gloss: Cooked by being covered completely in hot oil.
examples: The fair sells *deep-fried* Oreos.
I ordered the *deep-fried* shrimp.
Everything on this menu is *deep-fried*.

senses.gloss: Existing for a long time and very hard to change.
examples: The town has a *deep-rooted* distrust of outsiders.
Their love of baseball is *deep-rooted*.
The problem is more *deep-rooted* than we thought.

senses.gloss: In or from the deep parts of the ocean.
examples: We went *deep-sea* fishing off the coast of Florida.
*Deep-sea* divers need special training.
Some *deep-sea* creatures make their own light.

senses.gloss: Strongly felt or believed and difficult to change.
examples: She has a *deep-seated* fear of failure.
The conflict has *deep-seated* causes.
His anger seemed *deep-seated*.

senses.gloss: Of eyes: set far back in the face.
examples: He had dark, *deep-set* eyes.
Her eyes are *deep-set*, like her mother's.
The actor's *deep-set* eyes made him look serious.

senses.gloss: Becoming more serious, stronger or greater.
examples: The country faces a *deepening* economic crisis.
There is *deepening* concern about the water supply.
They watched the *deepening* shadows in the valley.

senses.gloss: Saying false things that damage someone's reputation.
examples: The senator sued the paper over a *defamatory* article.
The judge ruled that the posts were *defamatory*.
He was ordered to remove the *defamatory* statements from his website.

senses.gloss: Having lost a battle, game or election.
examples: The *defeated* army retreated to the hills.
The *defeated* candidate gave a short speech to her supporters.

senses.gloss: Feeling that you have failed and have no hope left.
examples: He walked off the field looking tired and *defeated*.
She sat at her desk with a *defeated* look on her face.
I've never felt more *defeated* in my life.

senses.gloss: Not made correctly or not working correctly.
examples: The store replaced the *defective* phone for free.
The car company recalled thousands of *defective* airbags.
If the heater is *defective*, send it back.

senses.gloss: Of a champion: having won the last competition and now trying to win again.
examples: The Chiefs are the *defending* Super Bowl champions.
The *defending* champion lost in the first round.
She is the *defending* title holder in the women's race.

senses.gloss: Weak and unable to protect yourself.
examples: The wolves attacked a *defenseless* calf.
Without a lawyer, he felt completely *defenseless*.
Newborn kittens are among the most *defenseless* animals.

senses.gloss: Able to be supported with good reasons.
examples: Firing him was a *defensible* decision.
Her position is legally *defensible*.
The second plan is more *defensible* than the first.

senses.gloss: Able to be protected from attack.
examples: The fort was built on a *defensible* hill.
The soldiers moved to a more *defensible* position.

senses.gloss: Used or done to protect against attack.
examples: The country says the missiles are purely *defensive*.
Take a *defensive* driving course to lower your insurance.

senses.gloss: Reacting as if you are being criticized or attacked.
examples: Why are you getting so *defensive*? I was only asking.
He gets *defensive* whenever his mother mentions his job.
She became more *defensive* with every question.

senses.gloss: In sports: trying to stop the other team from scoring.
examples: He plays on the *defensive* line.
It was the best *defensive* game of the season.

senses.gloss: Showing polite respect, often by agreeing with or obeying someone.
examples: The staff were very *deferential* to the new owner.
He spoke in a quiet, *deferential* voice.
Younger doctors were more *deferential* back then.

senses.gloss: Openly refusing to obey or to accept something.
examples: The teenager gave his father a *defiant* look.
Even after losing, the fans remained *defiant*.
The protesters grew more *defiant* as the police moved in.

contrast: Not Russian *дефицитный* (hard to find): *deficient* means lacking something needed. A scarce product is *hard to find* or *in short supply*.

senses.gloss: Not having enough of something that is needed.
examples: Many people are *deficient* in vitamin D in the winter.
The soil here is *deficient* in iron.
The report called the safety checks seriously *deficient*.

senses.gloss: Having a clear shape or outline.
examples: He's been working out and his arms are more *defined* now.
The shadows in the photo are sharply *defined*.

senses.gloss: Clearly stated, fixed or limited.
examples: Everyone on the team has a clearly *defined* role.
The contract runs for a *defined* period of two years.
The rules are not well *defined*.

senses.gloss: Having lost the air or gas inside.
examples: We found a *deflated* tire on the back of the car.
*Deflated* balloons lay all over the floor after the party.

senses.gloss: Suddenly less confident or less happy.
examples: I felt *deflated* when they didn't call me back.
The team looked *deflated* after the second goal.
She was more *deflated* by the silence than by the criticism.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *deflationary pressure*

senses.gloss: Causing or connected with a general fall in prices.
examples: The economy entered a *deflationary* period.
Falling oil prices had a *deflationary* effect.
Economists worry that the new policy is *deflationary*.

senses.gloss: Having a shape that is not normal or natural.
examples: The frog was born with a *deformed* leg.
The heat left the plastic cups *deformed*.
Some of the trees near the coast are badly *deformed* by the wind.

senses.gloss: Quick and skillful, with the hands or in handling a situation.
examples: With a few *deft* movements, she fixed the zipper.
He is *deft* at handling angry customers.
She has the *deftest* touch of any surgeon in the hospital.

senses.gloss: No longer existing, working or in business.
examples: He used to work for a now *defunct* airline.
The factory has been *defunct* since the 1990s.
The old law is *defunct* but was never officially removed.

contrast: The adjective ends in /ət/ (dih-JEN-ur-uht); the verb *to degenerate* ends in /eɪt/ (dih-JEN-uh-rayt). *A degenerate* is also a noun for a morally bad person.

senses.gloss: Morally bad, with low standards of behavior.
examples: Critics called the show *degenerate* trash.
He wasted his money on a *degenerate* lifestyle.
The city seemed more *degenerate* to him every year.

senses.gloss: Of a disease: slowly getting worse over time.
examples: Alzheimer's is a *degenerative* brain disease.
She suffers from *degenerative* arthritis in her knees.
There is still no cure for many *degenerative* conditions.

senses.gloss: Damaged or worse in quality than before.
examples: The river runs through badly *degraded* farmland.
The video signal was *degraded* by the storm.
This is one of the most *degraded* forests in the region.

senses.gloss: Feeling that you have lost respect or dignity.
examples: She felt *degraded* by the way they spoke to her.
The workers said they were treated like animals and felt *degraded*.

contrast: *degrading* describes the treatment (*a degrading job*); *degraded* describes how the person feels (*I felt degraded*).

senses.gloss: Making people lose respect for themselves or for others.
examples: Prisoners were forced to live in *degrading* conditions.
I find those ads *degrading* to women.
It was the most *degrading* experience of her career.

senses.gloss: Treated as if not a person, without kindness or respect.
examples: Many patients said they felt *dehumanized* in the hospital.
The film shows the *dehumanized* life of factory workers.
Refugees said the long lines and the numbers on their wrists left them feeling *dehumanized*.

senses.gloss: Of a person or body: having lost too much water.
examples: Drink plenty of water so you don't get *dehydrated*.
The hikers were badly *dehydrated* when they were found.
Small kids get *dehydrated* faster than adults.

senses.gloss: Of food: dried so that it keeps for a long time.
examples: We packed *dehydrated* meals for the camping trip.
Just add hot water to the *dehydrated* soup.

senses.gloss: Sad and disappointed.
examples: The *dejected* players sat in silence after the loss.
He looked *dejected* when she said no.
I've never seen him look more *dejected*.

senses.gloss: Happening or arriving later than planned or expected.
examples: Our flight to Denver is *delayed* again.
Passengers on the *delayed* train got free coffee.
Shock can cause a *delayed* reaction.

senses.gloss: Very pleasant, especially to taste.
examples: The bakery sells *delectable* peach pies.
Everything on the table looked *delectable*.
That was the most *delectable* meal I've had all year.

senses.gloss: Formal: causing harm or damage.
examples: Smoking has *deleterious* effects on your health.
The chemicals are *deleterious* to fish.
The new rules could be *deleterious* to small businesses.

contrast: The adjective ends in /ət/ (dih-LIB-ur-uht); the verb *to deliberate* ends in /eɪt/ (dih-LIB-uh-rayt) and means to think carefully before deciding.

senses.gloss: Done on purpose, not by accident.
examples: The fire was a *deliberate* attempt to destroy evidence.
That foul was *deliberate*.
It was a *deliberate* lie, not a mistake.

senses.gloss: Slow and careful.
examples: He walked to the stage with slow, *deliberate* steps.
Her speech was more *deliberate* than usual.

senses.gloss: Formed to discuss and decide things carefully.
examples: The Senate is often called the world's greatest *deliberative* body.
The jury began its *deliberative* process on Monday.
Town meetings are a form of *deliberative* democracy.

senses.gloss: Very pleasant or charming.
examples: We spent a *delightful* afternoon by the lake.
Your daughter is absolutely *delightful*.
It's one of the most *delightful* little restaurants in town.

contrast: *a delinquent* is also a noun, usually *a juvenile delinquent* (a young criminal).

senses.gloss: Of a young person: breaking the law or behaving badly.
senses.ru: с отклонениями в поведении, склонный к правонарушениям
examples: The program helps *delinquent* teenagers stay in school.
He was sent to a home for *delinquent* boys.

senses.gloss: Of a payment or account: late and not yet paid.
examples: The city is going after owners with *delinquent* property taxes.
Your account is 60 days *delinquent*.
The bank sold its *delinquent* loans to a collection agency.

ru: в бреду; вне себя от радости

senses.gloss: Confused and not thinking clearly, usually because of fever or illness.
examples: By midnight the child was *delirious* with fever.
He was *delirious* and didn't recognize his wife.

senses.gloss: Extremely excited or happy.
examples: *Delirious* fans ran onto the field after the win.
She was *delirious* with joy when she got the news.
The crowd got more *delirious* with every song.

senses.gloss: Believing things that are clearly not true.
examples: If he thinks he'll win, he's *delusional*.
The patient had *delusional* ideas about being watched.
Her plans get more *delusional* every week.

senses.gloss: Of higher quality and more expensive than the usual kind.
examples: We upgraded to a *deluxe* room with an ocean view.
The *deluxe* edition of the album has five extra songs.
I'll have the *deluxe* burger with fries.

senses.gloss: Winning support by playing on people's fears and emotions instead of using reason.
examples: The governor was known for his *demagogic* speeches.
Critics called the ad campaign *demagogic*.
His style became more *demagogic* as the election got closer.

senses.gloss: Needing a lot of time, effort or skill.
examples: Nursing is a physically *demanding* job.
The new position is more *demanding* than my old one.
Raising three kids alone is very *demanding*.

senses.gloss: Expecting a lot from other people.
examples: My boss is fair but very *demanding*.
She has some *demanding* clients.

senses.gloss: Making someone feel less respected or less important.
examples: He made a *demeaning* comment about her accent.
Having to beg for the money felt *demeaning*.
It was the most *demeaning* job I ever had.

senses.gloss: Informal: crazy or wildly strange.
examples: The movie is about a *demented* scientist.
He let out a *demented* laugh.
The plot gets more *demented* in the second season.

senses.gloss: Older medical use: suffering from dementia.
examples: In the past, *demented* patients were often locked away.
She cared for her *demented* father for ten years.

contrast: With a capital letter, *Democratic* means the US political party: *a Democratic senator*. With a small letter it means based on democracy.

senses.gloss: Based on a system where people choose their government by voting.
examples: The country held its first *democratic* elections in 1994.
Freedom of the press is essential in a *democratic* society.
The new constitution is more *democratic* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Treating everyone as equal and letting everyone have a say.
examples: The company has a very *democratic* way of making decisions.
Our family is pretty *democratic* — we vote on where to eat.

senses.gloss: Democratic: belonging to or supporting the Democratic Party in the US.
examples: She is running for the *Democratic* nomination.
The bill passed with *Democratic* votes.

contrast: *a demographic* is also a common noun in American English: a group of people of a certain age, income, etc. (*young voters are a key demographic*).

senses.gloss: Relating to the population and its structure by age, race, income and so on.
examples: The census gives us *demographic* data on every county.
The city is going through major *demographic* changes.
Advertisers study the *demographic* makeup of their audience.

senses.gloss: Of or like a demon; evil or wild.
examples: The priest believed the boy was under *demonic* control.
The villain had a *demonic* grin.
The music got faster and more *demonic*.

senses.gloss: Able to be clearly shown or proved.
examples: The new drug has no *demonstrable* benefits.
The claim is *demonstrable* with a simple test.
That statement is a *demonstrable* lie.

contrast: Not Russian *демонстративный* (done to be noticed, as in *демонстративно ушёл*). English *demonstrative* means showing love and affection openly. For the Russian sense, say *pointed* or *for show*.

senses.gloss: Openly showing your feelings, especially affection.
examples: My dad loved us, but he wasn't very *demonstrative*.

She greeted us with a *demonstrative* hug.

senses.gloss: In grammar: pointing to a particular thing, like *this*, *that*, *these* and *those*.
examples: "This" and "that" are *demonstrative* pronouns.

contrast: *demoralized* is how you feel (*the team was demoralized*); *demoralizing* is what causes it (*a demoralizing loss*).

senses.gloss: Having lost confidence and hope.

senses.gloss: Making people lose confidence and hope.

senses.gloss: Quiet, shy and modest, often in a way that seems proper.
examples: She gave him a *demure* smile.
The bride wore a *demure* white dress with long sleeves.
She was more *demure* in public than at home.

senses.gloss: Unfairly criticizing someone or treating them as unimportant.
examples: He made *denigrating* remarks about his opponent's family.
The comments were *denigrating* to immigrants.
It was the most *denigrating* review I've ever read.

senses.gloss: Thick or closely packed together; heavy for its size.
examples: The plane couldn't land because of *dense* fog.
Manhattan is one of the *densest* places in the country.

senses.gloss: Of writing: hard to understand because it has so many ideas.
examples: The textbook is too *dense* for beginners.

senses.gloss: Informal: slow to understand; stupid.

How can he be so *dense*?

senses.gloss: Relating to teeth or to the work of dentists.
examples: Does your job come with *dental* insurance?
I have a *dental* appointment on Friday.
Use *dental* floss every day.

senses.gloss: Having a small hollow in the surface from being hit or pressed.
examples: He drives an old truck with a *dented* fender.
The store won't sell *dented* cans.
My car door got *dented* in the parking lot.

senses.gloss: Relating to a department of a company, university or government.
examples: We have a *departmental* meeting every Tuesday.
The *departmental* budget was cut by ten percent.
She needs *departmental* approval to take the class.

senses.gloss: Able to be trusted to do what is needed.
examples: We need a *dependable* car for the drive to Texas.
Mike is always on time and very *dependable*.
It's the most *dependable* brand on the market.

senses.gloss: Much smaller in amount than before, or used up.
examples: The storm left the town's supplies badly *depleted*.
Farmers are struggling with *depleted* soil.
After the marathon, I felt completely *depleted*.

senses.gloss: Very bad and deserving strong criticism.
examples: The animals were kept in *deplorable* conditions.
His behavior at the game was *deplorable*.

contrast: Do not confuse with *deprived* (dih-PRYVD), which means lacking basic things: *a deprived childhood*.

senses.gloss: Morally very bad and evil.
examples: The killer was described as *depraved* and dangerous.
It was a *depraved* act of cruelty.
The villain gets more *depraved* in every book.

contrast: Do not confuse with *depraved* (dih-PRAYVD), which means morally evil.

senses.gloss: Poor and without the things people need, like good housing and education.
examples: The charity works with children from *deprived* backgrounds.

senses.gloss: Not having enough of something you need.

senses.gloss: Mentally ill and behaving in a wild or dangerous way.
examples: Police said the attacker was mentally *deranged*.

senses.gloss: Of a building or place: empty, not cared for and in bad condition.
examples: The kids played in a *derelict* warehouse by the river.

senses.gloss: Formal: failing to do what your job requires.
examples: The officers were *derelict* in their duty.
The report found the agency *derelict* in protecting children.

senses.gloss: Showing that you think someone or something is stupid or worthless.
examples: The crowd greeted his speech with *derisive* laughter.
She made a *derisive* noise when I mentioned the plan.
The critics were even more *derisive* about the sequel.

contrast: *a derivative* is also a noun: a word made from another word, a financial product, or a term in math.

senses.gloss: Copying other work too closely; not original.
examples: The band's first album was pretty *derivative*.
It's a *derivative* horror movie with no new ideas.
His later novels are more *derivative* than his early ones.

senses.gloss: Showing a low opinion of someone; insulting.
examples: He was fired for making *derogatory* comments about women.

senses.gloss: Going down, or arranged from the highest to the lowest.

We watched the *descending* plane circle the airport.

senses.gloss: Describing something, often in a clear and detailed way.

Give your files short but *descriptive* names.

senses.gloss: No longer separating people by race.

Students in the newly *desegregated* schools of the 1960s often faced hostility.
Years after the court ruling, many districts were still only partly *desegregated*.

senses.gloss: Empty, with no people in it.
examples: The streets were *deserted* after midnight.
They got stuck on a *deserted* road in Nevada.
The beach is even more *deserted* in November.

position: both — after a verb usually with *well* or *richly*: *The award was well deserved*

senses.gloss: Fairly earned by what someone has done.
examples: After the project, she took a well-*deserved* vacation.

senses.gloss: Worthy of help, praise or reward.
examples: The scholarship goes to a *deserving* student each year.

senses.gloss: Worth having or wanted by many people.
examples: They live in a very *desirable* neighborhood.

senses.gloss: Sexually attractive.
examples: The magazine named him one of the most *desirable* men in Hollywood.

senses.gloss: Wanted or hoped for.
examples: The warning had the *desired* effect, and the kids calmed down.

senses.gloss: Of a place: empty, bare and depressing.
examples: The road crosses a *desolate* stretch of desert.

senses.gloss: Of a person: very sad and lonely.

senses.gloss: Having lost hope and ready to try anything.

senses.gloss: Needing or wanting something very much.

senses.gloss: Of a situation: extremely serious or dangerous.
examples: The hospital is in *desperate* need of nurses.

senses.gloss: Extremely bad and deserving to be hated.

senses.gloss: Very unhappy and without hope.
examples: He became *despondent* after losing his job.

senses.gloss: Using power in a cruel and unfair way, with no limits.

senses.gloss: Certain to happen or to become something, as if decided by fate.

senses.gloss: Traveling toward or meant for a particular place.

senses.gloss: Extremely poor, without money, food or a home.

senses.gloss: Damaged so badly that it no longer exists or works.

senses.gloss: Informal: extremely upset or emotionally crushed.

senses.gloss: Causing a lot of damage or harm.

senses.gloss: Able to be removed and put back.
examples: The jacket has a *detachable* hood.

senses.gloss: Not emotionally involved; calm and distant.

senses.gloss: Of a building: standing alone, not joined to another.

senses.gloss: Including many small facts or parts.

senses.gloss: Able to be noticed or found.
examples: There was no *detectable* difference between the two samples.
The virus is *detectable* in the blood after a week.
The smell became more *detectable* as the day got warmer.

senses.gloss: Having firmly decided to do something and not letting anything stop you.
examples: She was *determined* to finish college.
He's a very *determined* young man.
The loss only made the team more *determined*.

senses.gloss: Deciding how something will happen or end.
examples: Price was the *determining* factor in our choice.
Location is often the *determining* issue when buying a house.
Weather played a *determining* role in the battle.

senses.gloss: Very unpleasant and deserving to be hated.
examples: Cruelty to animals is *detestable*.
He was a *detestable* man who cheated his own brother.
It was one of the most *detestable* crimes of the decade.

senses.gloss: Causing harm or damage.
examples: Too much screen time can be *detrimental* to kids' sleep.
The tax would have a *detrimental* effect on small farms.
Stress is more *detrimental* to your health than you think.

senses.gloss: Of money: officially made worth less.
examples: Imports became expensive because of the *devalued* peso.
A *devalued* dollar makes American goods cheaper abroad.

senses.gloss: Of a person or their work: not respected or valued enough.
examples: Many teachers feel *devalued* and underpaid.
Housework is still a *devalued* form of labor.
Nurses said they had never felt more *devalued*.

contrast: *devastating* is what causes the shock (*devastating news*); *devastated* is how you feel (*I was devastated*).

senses.gloss: Causing very great damage.
examples: The *devastating* fire destroyed over a thousand homes.
The drought had a *devastating* effect on crops.
It was the most *devastating* storm in fifty years.

senses.gloss: Very shocking and upsetting.
examples: Losing her mother was *devastating*.
They received the *devastating* news on Christmas Eve.

senses.gloss: Informal: very impressive or powerful.
examples: She has a *devastating* smile.
He answered with *devastating* wit.

senses.gloss: Of a country: rich, with a lot of industry and modern services.
examples: The US and Japan are *developed* countries.
Cancer rates are higher in the more *developed* parts of the world.

senses.gloss: Grown or advanced to a high level.
examples: Dogs have a highly *developed* sense of smell.
The plan isn't fully *developed* yet.
Her singing voice is well *developed* for a twelve-year-old.

senses.gloss: Of a country: poorer and still building its industry and services.
examples: Many *developing* countries lack clean water.
The loan program helps farmers in the *developing* world.

senses.gloss: Growing or changing, and not yet complete.
examples: This is a *developing* story, and we'll have more details soon.
Alcohol can harm a *developing* baby.
Teenagers still have *developing* brains.

senses.gloss: Relating to the way a person, especially a child, grows and develops.
examples: The clinic treats children with *developmental* delays.
Walking is an important *developmental* milestone.
She studies *developmental* psychology.

contrast: *a deviant* is also a noun, often an insult for a person whose behavior (especially sexual) is seen as abnormal.

senses.gloss: Different from what most people think is normal or acceptable.
examples: The study looks at *deviant* behavior in teenagers.
In the 1950s, long hair on men was seen as *deviant*.
His views became more *deviant* over the years.
